bull.b: Very low leverage reduces near-term balance-sheet risk and limits the burden of interest or mandatory debt repayment. This gives Tenaya more flexibility to direct available capital toward clinical development and preserves financing options as its programs advance.

Moving future AAV manufacturing to an external provider reduces long-term facility obligations while retaining internal process and assay expertise. The model can improve capital efficiency and allow production capacity to scale more flexibly if clinical programs progress.

Adding a CFO with senior roles at multiple biotechnology companies strengthens financial oversight during a capital-intensive development period. Better capital allocation and corporate-development execution could support disciplined funding of programs and longer-term strategic flexibility.

bear.b: Sustained negative operating and free cash flow means Tenaya currently consumes capital rather than funding operations internally. Continued development spending will require effective cost control and access to additional financing before products can generate meaningful cash.

Large losses relative to still-minimal revenue show that Tenaya remains far from sustainable profitability. The company must convert clinical investment into successful products or partnerships, while prolonged losses can constrain strategic options and increase funding dependence.

The substantial reduction in equity indicates that ongoing losses have consumed a meaningful portion of the capital base. A smaller equity cushion leaves less internal financial capacity for lengthy clinical programs and heightens the importance of future capital allocation discipline.
